subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with regurgitation and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 42 year old woman referred with eighteen months of food sticking. She describes the sensation behind the lower sternum and says it happens just as much with water as with steak, and that she now eats standing up and drinks fizzy water to push food down.

She brings up undigested food on the pillow at night and has lost 5 kg. She was treated for reflux with esomeprazole for six months with no benefit. She has never smoked and takes no other medicines.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non tender with no mass, no oral candidiasis
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained saliva and food residue in the oesophagus, a normal oesophageal mucosa with no rings, furrows or stricture, and mild resistance on passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yields with gentle pressure, biopsies from the distal oesophagus showing no eosinophilic infiltrate, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry with assessment of relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal mucosa, points to a motility disorder, and manometry is the test that establishes failure of relaxation at the junction with absent peristalsis and subclassifies the pattern. That subclassification matters because it predicts the response to dilatation, myotomy and botulinum toxin. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppressing therapy
options.rationale: Ambulatory reflux monitoring quantifies acid exposure and correlates symptoms with reflux episodes, which is useful for refractory heartburn or before antireflux surgery. It does not assess peristalsis or junction relaxation and would not explain dysphagia to liquids. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen with intravenous contrast to look for an infiltrating lesion
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is used when malignancy at or near the junction is suspected, typically with rapid progression over weeks in an older patient and a mucosal abnormality at endoscopy. It has a place later if manometry shows a pattern suggesting an infiltrating tumour mimicking a primary motility disorder. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: A further eight week course of a high dose proton pump inhibitor taken twice daily before meals
options.rationale: She has already failed six months of acid suppression, and retained food with dysphagia to liquids is not a reflux pattern. Repeating a failed therapeutic trial delays a diagnosis that has now been symptomatic for eighteen months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: A timed barium swallow with fluoroscopic screening of the oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: A barium study can show a dilated oesophagus with a tapered bird beak appearance and is a useful adjunct, particularly for assessing emptying before and after treatment, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis and it cannot subclassify the disorder. Manometry remains the reference standard. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

explanation.summary: Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and oesophageal peristalsis is lost, producing dysphagia that is present for liquids as well as solids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, chest discomfort and weight loss. This liquid and solid pattern is the key discriminator from a mechanical stricture or tumour, which typically causes solid food dysphagia first. Endoscopy is performed in every patient to exclude mucosal disease and pseudoachalasia from a tumour infiltrating the junction, and retained food with mild resistance at the junction is a supportive but non specific finding. High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and defines the subtype, which guides treatment between pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy and, in those unfit for procedures, botulinum toxin injection. Long standing disease carries a small increased risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and treatment relieves obstruction without restoring peristalsis, so reflux management after myotomy is part of ongoing care.
key_points: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction.
Endoscopy is done first to exclude mucosal disease and a tumour infiltrating the junction.
High resolution manometry is the reference standard and subclassifies the disorder to guide treatment.
Barium studies support the diagnosis and assess emptying but cannot exclude it or subtype it.
Failure to respond to an adequate trial of acid suppression argues against reflux as the explanation.
explanation.pearls: Pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction is suggested by symptoms of under six months, weight loss out of proportion to the dysphagia, and age over sixty, and in that combination cross sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound follows manometry even when the mucosa looked normal.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

subtopic_detail: Recurrent food bolus obstruction in a young atopic man planned for endoscopy after spontaneous passage
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 26 year old man in clinic after his second presentation to the emergency department with meat lodged in his oesophagus, which passed spontaneously after an hour both times.

Between episodes he eats slowly, chews carefully and avoids bread and steak at restaurants. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever each spring, and had eczema as a child. Acid suppression for three months made no difference to his swallowing. You are booking his gastroscopy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, chest clear with no wheeze, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no oral lesions, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), previous gastroscopy report from another centre describing linear furrows and concentric rings with no stricture and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange a timed barium swallow to define the calibre of the oesophagus before any further endoscopic procedure
options.rationale: A barium study can outline a narrow calibre oesophagus but cannot make a diagnosis that depends on counting eosinophils in tissue. It is reserved for assessing strictures and planning dilatation rather than for establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Proceed to gastroscopy and take at least six oesophageal biopsies from both the proximal and the distal oesophagus
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field in oesophageal tissue, disease is patchy, and the yield rises with the number of biopsies, so six or more specimens from two levels is the standard sampling strategy. Biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal, because up to a fifth of affected patients have no endoscopic abnormality. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Refer him for skin prick testing to common foods and start an elimination diet based on the results obtained
options.rationale: Allergy testing performs poorly at predicting which foods drive this condition, and dietary therapy is guided by empirical elimination of common trigger groups with endoscopic reassessment rather than by test results. Diet is also a treatment decision that follows histological confirmation. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Eosinophilic oesophagitis

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to assess peristalsis and relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: Manometry investigates dysphagia to liquids as well as solids with regurgitation, a pattern typical of achalasia, whereas his obstruction occurs only with solid boluses and his previous endoscopy showed rings and furrows. Motility testing would not detect the mucosal disease being tested for. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Start a topical swallowed corticosteroid preparation now and reassess his symptoms in the clinic after eight weeks
options.rationale: Swallowed topical corticosteroid is an established first line treatment but starting it before biopsies are taken removes the histological evidence needed to confirm the diagnosis and to judge response. Treatment follows tissue confirmation in this condition. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease that has become the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults, typically men with a personal or family history of atopy. Symptoms are solid food dysphagia and bolus impaction, often with years of adaptive behaviours such as eating slowly, over chewing, drinking with meals and avoiding dense foods, which patients rarely volunteer unless asked. Diagnosis requires symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction with at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field on biopsy, and because the infiltrate is patchy the standard is six or more biopsies taken from proximal and distal levels, including when the mucosa appears normal. Treatment options are proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone preparations, empirical dietary elimination, and dilatation for fibrotic strictures, with repeat biopsy used to confirm histological remission because symptoms alone underestimate ongoing inflammation. Untreated inflammation leads to subepithelial fibrosis and a narrow calibre oesophagus over years, so maintenance therapy is the rule rather than the exception.
key_points: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults and is strongly associated with atopy.
Diagnosis needs at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy.
Disease is patchy, so at least six biopsies are taken from proximal and distal oesophagus, even if the mucosa looks normal.
Peripheral eosinophilia is neither sensitive nor specific and cannot substitute for tissue sampling.
Symptoms underestimate inflammation, so histological reassessment guides maintenance therapy.
explanation.pearls: Adaptive eating behaviours are the most useful history in this condition: a young man who cuts food into tiny pieces, always has a glass of water at the table and lets everyone else finish first has had oesophageal narrowing for years even if he denies dysphagia.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

subtopic_detail: Progressive magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild cognitive slowing alongside ventriculomegaly on imaging
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 76 year old man referred with eighteen months of unsteadiness. His wife says his feet seem stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and he has had three falls in six months.

He has become slower in conversation and now has to hurry to the toilet, with two episodes of incontinence. He has no tremor, his handwriting is unchanged, and he has never had a stroke or head injury. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin only.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with reduced step height and difficulty initiating, turning by small steps taking five steps to turn, arm swing preserved, no resting tremor, tone normal without cogwheeling, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 24 out of 30 with losses in executive and attention items, no focal weakness, reflexes symmetrical, plantar responses flexor
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showing symmetrically enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.37, narrowed callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci with only mild cortical atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer him directly for insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt on the basis of his symptoms and imaging findings
options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment but carries risks of infection, subdural haematoma and overdrainage, so patient selection rests on demonstrating that cerebrospinal fluid removal actually improves gait rather than on imaging appearances alone. Imaging findings like these are also seen in people who do not respond to shunting. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Commence a trial of levodopa with carbidopa and assess his gait and turning after four weeks of treatment
options.rationale: A levodopa trial is used when the picture suggests parkinsonism, which typically brings asymmetric bradykinesia, rigidity with cogwheeling, reduced arm swing and a resting tremor, none of which he has. Gait apraxia with preserved arm swing and normal tone points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Arrange a large volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and after the cerebrospinal fluid is removed
options.rationale: Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and formally measuring gait speed and a timed walk before and several hours after is the standard test of whether this gait will respond to shunting, and a clear improvement predicts benefit. It also excludes raised opening pressure and allows cerebrospinal fluid analysis for alternative causes. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for his cognitive impairment and review his cognition and function in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies and have no role in a potentially reversible hydrocephalic picture, and his cognitive deficits are executive rather than amnestic. Starting one here would delay a treatable diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer him for urodynamic studies and start an antimuscarinic agent for his urinary urgency and incontinence
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the unifying explanation for gait, cognition and continence, and antimuscarinics worsen cognition in older adults. Urinary symptoms in this syndrome improve when the underlying problem is treated. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a potentially reversible cause of gait disturbance in older people, characterised by the triad of a magnetic apraxic gait, urinary urgency and incontinence, and subcortical cognitive slowing, with gait usually the earliest and most shunt responsive feature. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy, commonly quantified by an Evans index above 0.3, with a narrowed callosal angle and crowded sulci at the high convexity. Because ventricular enlargement also accompanies cerebral atrophy and other neurodegenerative disease, imaging alone cannot select patients for surgery, and a supplementary test of cerebrospinal fluid removal is used: a large volume lumbar puncture with objective gait measurement before and after, or extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases. Patients who improve after fluid removal have substantially higher rates of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, with gait improving most reliably and cognition least. The main differentials are vascular parkinsonism, Parkinson disease, and cervical myelopathy, and the practical error is attributing a treatable gait disorder to age or to dementia.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest and most shunt responsive element of the triad.
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, with a narrowed callosal angle, supports the diagnosis.
Imaging cannot select surgical candidates, so a cerebrospinal fluid removal test is performed.
Objective timed gait measurement before and after the tap is what makes the test interpretable.
Preserved arm swing with normal tone argues against Parkinson disease as the cause.
explanation.pearls: Measure the gait formally with a timed ten metre walk and a timed up and go before the tap and again three to four hours afterwards, because subjective impressions from the patient and family after a lumbar puncture are unreliable and a documented improvement of around twenty per cent is what drives the neurosurgical referral.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

subtopic_detail: Persistent watery diarrhoea after stopping the implicated drug in a woman whose colonoscopy was macroscopically normal
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman eight weeks after her colonoscopy. She has had six months of watery diarrhoea, six to eight times a day including at night, with urgency but no blood.

Her colonoscopy looked normal to the eye and random biopsies showed a thickened subepithelial collagen band with a lymphocytic infiltrate. She stopped the diclofenac she had been taking for knee pain the day after the procedure and has had no improvement in eight weeks. Her weight is stable and she has coeliac serology that was negative with a normal immunoglobulin A.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with no mass, no perianal disease, no oedema, no goitre, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, faecal calprotectin within normal limits, stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, colonic biopsies showing a thickened subepithelial collagen band with chronic inflammation and preserved crypt architecture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Commence mesalazine 3 g daily and review her stool frequency and inflammatory markers after 8 weeks
options.rationale: Mesalazine performs poorly in this condition compared with budesonide in randomised comparisons and is not recommended as first line. Its established role is in ulcerative colitis, in which the mucosa is macroscopically abnormal and crypt architecture is distorted. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Prescribe loperamide 2 mg titrated to stool frequency and review her in the outpatient clinic in 3 months
options.rationale: Antidiarrhoeal therapy is a reasonable adjunct and is sometimes sufficient for mild disease, but it controls the symptom without treating the mucosal inflammation in a woman whose nocturnal diarrhoea is disrupting her life. It is generally used alongside or after the agent that induces remission. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Arrange a repeat colonoscopy with extensive random biopsies from the right and left colon to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already secure on histology from a macroscopically normal colon, which is exactly how this condition is identified. Repeating the procedure exposes her to risk and delays treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Commence oral budesonide at 9 mg daily for eight weeks and then taper according to her symptomatic response
options.rationale: Budesonide is the treatment with the strongest randomised evidence for inducing remission in microscopic colitis, with response rates around eighty per cent, and its high first pass metabolism limits systemic corticosteroid effects. Treatment is indicated here because withdrawal of the implicated drug alone has not worked over an adequate interval. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Commence a bile acid sequestrant and arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan if she does not respond
options.rationale: Bile acid diarrhoea is an important cause of chronic watery diarrhoea and coexists with this condition in some patients, so sequestrants are used as second line therapy. It does not explain the histological findings already documented on her biopsies. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a common and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery non bloody diarrhoea, particularly in women over fifty, and comprises collagenous colitis, defined by a thickened subepithelial collagen band, and lymphocytic colitis, defined by increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. The colon looks normal at colonoscopy, which is why random biopsies from the right and left colon are mandatory in the investigation of chronic diarrhoea even when the mucosa appears unremarkable. Nocturnal diarrhoea, urgency and faecal incontinence are typical and distinguish it clinically from irritable bowel syndrome, and it is associated with coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease and with drugs including non steroidal anti inflammatory agents, proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and statins. Management begins with stopping implicated drugs, and budesonide is the first line agent for inducing remission with response rates around eighty per cent, although relapse after withdrawal is common and some patients need maintenance therapy. Second line options include bile acid sequestrants, and immunomodulators or biologic therapy are reserved for refractory disease.
key_points: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy requires random biopsies to make the diagnosis.
Nocturnal diarrhoea and urgency point away from irritable bowel syndrome.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and statins are recognised triggers.
Budesonide is first line for induction, with response rates around eighty per cent and limited systemic effects.
Relapse after stopping treatment is common and some patients require maintenance therapy.
explanation.pearls: Check coeliac serology in every patient diagnosed with microscopic colitis, because coeliac disease coexists in up to one in five and diarrhoea that fails to respond to budesonide is frequently explained by untreated gluten sensitive enteropathy.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update
